newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai economy shows no recovery signs - central bank.
newsitem.headline: Thai economy shows no recovery signs - central bank.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand said on Thursday it still saw no clear signs of a turnaround of the country's economic slowdown despite moderate export growth in January.

Central bank chief economist Kleo-thong Hetrakul said 5.1 percent year-on-year export growth in January was offset by higher imports of industrial raw materials and petroleum which widened the trade deficit to its highest level in nine months.
"It is still not clear that the economy has recovered...even though exports showed a better outlook," she told reporters.
The central bank also said the balance of payments switched to a 26.6 billion baht ($1.02 billion) deficit in February from a 24.7 billion baht surplus in the previous month.

The bank economist blamed the February capital outflow on market attacks on the baht during the first three weeks of last month. She declined to say how much foreign exchange the central bank had used to intervene to defend the baht.
Thai foreign reserves fell to $38.1 billion at end-February from $39.2 billion a month earlier and $38.7 billion a year ago.
"Every growth indicator remained weak including industrial production, private investment and bank lending," said an analyst at Multi-Credit Corp of Thailand Plc.
The central bank said the manufacturing production index extended its weak growth, rising only about 4.0 percent year-on-year in January, its lowest in about a decade.

"How can we expect the gross domestic product (GDP) to grow seven to eight percent this year when industrial output rose only four percent. I expect February industrial production to be even lower which may leave whole year economic growth at about 5.5 percent," the Multi-Credit analyst said.
Thai GDP expanded 6.7 percent in 1996 against 8.7 in 1995.

Analysts said market focus on the economy had shifted to Thailand's growth prospect from earlier concerns over the current account deficit which stood at 8.0 percent of GDP in 1996. Kleo-thong said the deficit could narrow to about seven percent this year.
The central bank said private investment stayed on a steady lower growth trend in January. It rose 7.3 percent year-on-year during the month against 7.5 in December and 13.4 a year ago.
"I think the current weak domestic consumer demand would take longer time to pick up than exports," said another analyst.

The central bank said the January current account deficit widened to 22.5 billion baht from 19.1 billion in December but Kleo-thong described the latest figure as satisfactory comparing with a monthly peak of 49.6 billion baht in April 1996.

Kleo-thong said January imports surged to about 154.9 billion baht, a monthly high since May 1996 and against 139.3 billion in December, as factories increased imports of petroleum and raw materials in response to government tariff cuts.

She said January exports amounted to about 115.9 billion baht against 117.0 billion in December. The January figure was, however, 5.1 percent higher than a year ago, after it contracted year-on-year in each of the previous seven months.
January's trade deficit soared to a preliminary 39.0 billion baht from 22.3 billion in December but against 42.6 billion a year ago.
